#6160. Airbnb Sells IP to AI Lab Owned by Its CEO and CTO

Airbnb’s CEO and CTO both own part of the lab buying its IP, but the filing gives shareholders little detail on what changed hands.

Airbnb sold intellectual property to a private AI lab founded and controlled by CEO Brian Chesky. CTO Ahmad Al-Dahle also holds a stake in the lab, and both executives work for the entity.

The November transaction generated $7.1 million in cash for the IP and expense reimbursements combined, according to Airbnb’s quarterly SEC filing.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Airbnb disclosed in its quarterly SEC filing that it sold intellectual property to a private AI lab founded and controlled by CEO Brian Chesky, with CTO Ahmad Al-Dahle holding a stake and both executives working for the entity. The November transaction brought Airbnb $7.1 million in cash covering the IP and expense reimbursements combined, and a special committee of independent, disinterested directors approved it under the company's related-party transaction policy. In return, Airbnb received a license to certain lab IP for internal use and the right to invest in future equity rounds, though the filing does not identify the IP, explain its valuation, separate the purchase price from expenses, or disclose the license economics. Airbnb said the executives' roles at the lab will not change their responsibilities to the company. The arrangement lands as Airbnb prepares a proprietary AI travel agent for the first half of 2027, built to assemble maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, and itineraries around guest queries. Neither the filing nor the shareholder update says whether that agent draws on the lab's technology, or whether the lab could license the same IP to competitors such as Booking Holdings or Expedia.

#6159. Uber Wants You To Drive Yourself—Reserve Parking In 15 Cities, Earn 10% Back

Uber is launching parking reservations in 15 U.S. cities, letting you find a garage or lot, compare prices, and pay inside its app. Uber One members earn 10% back in credits on eligible bookings and of course Uber One comes with Amex Platinum. It’s a little weird to have self-service Uber. You supply the car. You do the driving. But they offer Uber Eats for pickup, so I guess? Still, even if it’s not gig workers and urban mobility, if the price and rebate are good, ok then. Where Uber Parking Is Available Uber’s November 9 launch covers Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, D.C. They plan to expand across the United States. This follows Uber’s acquisition of SpotHero, announced in February. SpotHero’s broader network has more than 13,000 garages, lots, and valet locations across over 400 cities in the U.S. and Canada. However, Uber’s parking page lists 7,000 facilities. Tap Parking in the Uber app, enter your destination and parking times, and compare the map’s prices. You can filter for self-parking or valet, garages or surface lots, and things like on-site staff. Enter your vehicle details and license plate, pay via your Uber Wallet, and follow the entry instructions on the parking pass. Uber already has your account and payment information. SpotHero had parking reservations. Now it’s in one place with Uber rebates. 10% Rebate, Including Taxes And Fees Uber One members earn 10% credits on eligible completed parking reservations including the parking charge, taxes, and fees. Credits generally arrive within 24 hours after the reservation. Not every location or reservation qualifies. Uber One costs $9.99 a month or $96 a year. Buying an annual membership solely for parking requires $960 in eligible annual parking purchases just to earn $96 in credits, assuming you use those credits at full value. So this is for someone who already has Uber One. Can You Use Amex Uber Cash? And Does Amazon Help? Uber Cash works at supported parking locations. Uber’s parking help page says so, and Uber’s American Express terms say: The Amex Benefit may be applied to any services to which Uber permits Uber Cash to be applied. So this is a new way to use monthly Uber credits ($15 monthly, plus another $20 in December). Consumer Gold offers $10 monthly. And you can get Uber One via Amex Platinum: up to $120 in statement credits per calendar year for membership fees charged directly to the card. Both monthly and annual plans qualify. (Consumer Centurion cards have a membership credit as well.) Keep Uber Cash off for the membership payment so Amex is charged and can reimburse it. Amazon Prime doesn’t unlock this. The new U.S. Amazon arrangement provides $0 delivery fees on eligible Uber Eats restaurant orders of $25 or more placed through Amazon, but doesn’t give you an Uber One membership. Those orders use a separate account and Uber One benefits don’t apply to them. Uber Isn’t The Only Option In This Market There are plenty of alternatives. Alternative   What To Compare SpotHero directly   The same underlying parking business, with a broader geographic footprint and hourly, monthly, event, and airport parking. ParkWhiz and BestParking   Other booking channels for prepaid garage and lot reservations, including event parking. ParkMobile and PayByPhone   Useful for paying for and extending parking in participating locations. ParkMobile also offers advance reservations. AirportParkingReservations.com and Way.com   Airport parking comparisons, including off-airport lots and hotel parking. Compare shuttle schedules, operating hours, and cancellation rules. The garage, hotel, event venue, or airport directly   Prepaid offers, parking packages, validation, and loyalty discounts that might beat an intermediary’s price. I’ve written about the economics of empty parking spaces: the garage already exists, and an unsold hour is revenue the operator never gets back. Advance booking can give operators a way to discount to people who compare prices while charging more to drivers who just show up. Uber says many participating locations offer rates below their drive-up prices. Read The Parking Pass Before You Pay Uber’s parking rules leave several decisions to the individual facility: Cancellation. Uber says most options can be canceled free before the start time, but the deadline shown for your reservation controls. Extensions. Most active reservations can be extended if space is available but don’t assume you can stay indefinitely at the original rate. Entry and exit. Follow the pass’s barcode, license plate, or attendant instructions. Most participating facilities don’t allow repeated entry and exit during one reservation. Vehicle restrictions and extra charges. Check height limits and oversized vehicle charges, along with early entry and late exit rules. Uber’s charge guidance flags additional fees. A reservation doesn’t imply a particular space is being held. SpotHero says it manages inventory with operators rather than physically holding a specific stall. If you arrive and can’t enter or the lot is full, Uber directs you to the parking pass’s help option. Good luck. There are two other launch limitations in Uber’s FAQ: business profiles aren’t supported, and Uber and SpotHero accounts can’t be linked. An Uber reservation won’t appear in your SpotHero account. The claim in the launch pitch that Americans spend an average of 17 hours a year looking for parking comes from a July 2017 study. It seems to me there’s very high variance in this. In fact, isn’t one solution just to Uber? Uber gets a transaction from people who choose to drive, then offers credits that encourage them to come back for a ride or food order. They also say they’ll explore using parking locations to stage autonomous vehicles between trips. They’re going to be losing their Waymo partnership so I wonder what that looks like? What I’d Really Like Is Uber Valet About a decade ago, Luxe offered a valet would meet you at your destination, take your car away to park it, and bring it back when you were ready. Zirx did, too. Walking into a restaurant while somebody dealt with your car was super value add! But it’s a tough business. Luxe ended its consumer valet service in 2017, and Volvo bought its technology, team, and other assets that September. Zirx stopped consumer valet service in February 2016. Attendants had to reach customers, park their cars, and return them, on top of paying for parking and insurance. Uber considered buying Luxe’s assets and engineers before Volvo did. Valet Network in New York advertises $10 parking, using street spaces. Apparently the service is in Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, and the Lower East Side and it’s another $3 to return the car. Ector offers something like this at French airports and train stations. That seems like an Uber feature, this is more like selling hotels through the app because they already have customers and their customers travel. I liked the old Travis vision for the company so much better. They had some growing up to do and maybe they wouldn’t have achieved everything before the VC cash ran out but this just isn’t that exciting of a vision, even if you have something new to do with existing Uber credits. I’ve written about the economics of empty parking spaces: the garage already exists, and an unsold hour is revenue the operator never gets back. Advance booking can give operators a way to discount to people who compare prices while charging more to drivers who just show up. Uber says many participating locations offer rates below their drive-up prices.

Uber’s parking rules leave several decisions to the individual facility: Cancellation. Uber says most options can be canceled free before the start time, but the deadline shown for your reservation controls. Extensions. Most active reservations can be extended if space is available but don’t assume you can stay indefinitely at the original rate. Entry and exit. Follow the pass’s barcode, license plate, or attendant instructions. Most participating facilities don’t allow repeated entry and exit during one reservation. Vehicle restrictions and extra charges. Check height limits and oversized vehicle charges, along with early entry and late exit rules. Uber’s charge guidance flags additional fees. A reservation doesn’t imply a particular space is being held. SpotHero says it manages inventory with operators rather than physically holding a specific stall. If you arrive and can’t enter or the lot is full, Uber directs you to the parking pass’s help option. Good luck. There are two other launch limitations in Uber’s FAQ: business profiles aren’t supported, and Uber and SpotHero accounts can’t be linked. An Uber reservation won’t appear in your SpotHero account. The claim in the launch pitch that Americans spend an average of 17 hours a year looking for parking comes from a July 2017 study. It seems to me there’s very high variance in this. In fact, isn’t one solution just to Uber? Uber gets a transaction from people who choose to drive, then offers credits that encourage them to come back for a ride or food order. They also say they’ll explore using parking locations to stage autonomous vehicles between trips. They’re going to be losing their Waymo partnership so I wonder what that looks like? What I’d Really Like Is Uber Valet About a decade ago, Luxe offered a valet would meet you at your destination, take your car away to park it, and bring it back when you were ready. Zirx did, too. Walking into a restaurant while somebody dealt with your car was super value add! But it’s a tough business. Luxe ended its consumer valet service in 2017, and Volvo bought its technology, team, and other assets that September. Zirx stopped consumer valet service in February 2016. Attendants had to reach customers, park their cars, and return them, on top of paying for parking and insurance. Uber considered buying Luxe’s assets and engineers before Volvo did. Valet Network in New York advertises $10 parking, using street spaces. Apparently the service is in Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, and the Lower East Side and it’s another $3 to return the car. Ector offers something like this at French airports and train stations. That seems like an Uber feature, this is more like selling hotels through the app because they already have customers and their customers travel. I liked the old Travis vision for the company so much better. They had some growing up to do and maybe they wouldn’t have achieved everything before the VC cash ran out but this just isn’t that exciting of a vision, even if you have something new to do with existing Uber credits. #6155. Aviation’s Next Disaster Could Be In Your Carry-On

Battery incidents are rising and airlines are tightening restrictions, with cabin crews the last line of defense. Is the industry doing enough to prevent the next fire, or simply getting better at putting them out?

The culprit was small enough to fit in a pocket, but the consequences were big enough to turn a Boeing 777 around over the Atlantic.

On September 17, a portable charger caught fire aboard KLM flight 735 from Amsterdam to Curaçao. The crew extinguished the flames and the jet returned safely to the Dutch capital. One person was injured and the incident led to knock-on cancellations, overnight accommodation for hundreds of passengers, and the plane being out of service until September 20.

An intriguing twist soon followed when Dutch media reported that the device allegedly belonged to Camiel Eurlings, KLM's former chief executive. The airline has declined to identify the passenger and Eurlings did not respond to Skift’s request for comment. On November 4, the Dutch Safety Board opened an independent investigation into the incident.

The reported CEO connection attracted international tabloid attention, but the passenger's identity is secondary to a broa

A portable charger fire aboard KLM flight 735 from Amsterdam to Curaçao on September 17 forced the Boeing 777 to turn back, injured one person, triggered cancellations, and kept the aircraft out of service until September 20. Dutch media reported the device allegedly belonged to former KLM CEO Camiel Eurlings; the airline declined to identify the passenger, and the Dutch Safety Board opened an investigation on November 4. The incident sits inside a sharply worsening trend. The UK Civil Aviation Authority estimates the average passenger now carries four lithium-powered devices, and its reports of passenger devices overheating rose 98% between 2024 and 2025. The FAA logged 97 lithium-battery incidents involving smoke, fire, or extreme heat in 2025, against 47 in 2017, and deputy director Paul Serafin said the agency has recently seen roughly two incidents a week on passenger aircraft. UL Standards & Engagement estimates an average cost of about $96,000 per event, with about 12% of incidents in its dataset resulting in a diversion or emergency landing. New ICAO provisions that took effect at the end of March cap passengers at two power banks and prohibit recharging them in flight, but implementation varies by jurisdiction and airlines can set stricter limits. Battery safety expert Paul Christensen said the airline industry needs to wake up as a matter of extreme urgency; IATA's Jonathan Jasper cautioned that most reports involve overheating rather than full thermal runaway.

#6153. Flight Attendant Finds Hidden Camera In Lavatory—Passenger Charged With Trying To Erase Evidence

A flight attendant found a hidden camera in a Scoot lavatory. The passenger onboard the Singapore Airlines low cost carrier accused of putting it there is also charged with deleting evidence. It’s the deleting that creates the greatest risk of imprisonment. The incident happened October 7 on Scoot flight TR821 from Osaka to Singapore. The 52-year-old British passenger was charged in Singapore on November 5. One Mile at a Time flags the story noting he’s currently jailed. He’s now been offered S$10,000 bail. The man plans to plead guilty. According to the Singapore Police Force, the man concealed a camera in a lavatory, left, and activated recording through an app on his phone. A female flight attendant discovered the device while using the lavatory. She removed it and alerted a colleague. Police say Lutley later tried to retrieve it, found it missing, and deleted the app and related photographs to avoid detection. Officers detained him when the flight arrived at Changi Airport and seized both his phone and the camera. That’s some fancy police work! The Alleged Deletion Carries The Biggest Penalty He faces one count each of: Voyeurism: up to two years in prison, with a fine also available. Obstructing the course of justice: up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both, over the alleged deletion of the app and photographs. While the voyeurism law includes caning, Singapore exempts men over 50 so he’s in the clear there. The United Airlines Passenger Who Recorded Himself In 2019, I wrote about a United Airlines passenger accused of hiding a camera in the first class lavatory on a San Diego – Houston flight. A woman found the device and handed it to a flight attendant. The camera had recorded the man installing it. Investigators matched his clothing and jewelry to airport footage. They also recovered deleted files showing women in an Emirates lavatory, including a flight attendant. And there’s the American Airlines case where a family alleged the airline gave a flight attendant time to erase evidence after a teenage passenger discovered his phone attached to a toilet seat with maintenance stickers. Federal prosecutors later confirmed that the crewmember had reset his phone, while investigators found recordings of other children in his cloud account. He received an 18 1/2 year prison sentence last year. In 2019, I wrote about a United Airlines passenger accused of hiding a camera in the first class lavatory on a San Diego – Houston flight. A woman found the device and handed it to a flight attendant.

The camera had recorded the man installing it. Investigators matched his clothing and jewelry to airport footage. They also recovered deleted files showing women in an Emirates lavatory, including a flight attendant.

And there’s the American Airlines case where a family alleged the airline gave a flight attendant time to erase evidence after a teenage passenger discovered his phone attached to a toilet seat with maintenance stickers.

Federal prosecutors later confirmed that the crewmember had reset his phone, while investigators found recordings of other children in his cloud account. He received an 18 1/2 year prison sentence last year.

If you've ever rented a car, you've probably been asked whether you want to pay extra for insurance at the counter. But depending on which credit card you have, you may already have some coverage.

Many travel rewards credit cards offer rental car insurance that can protect you against theft or damage to your rental vehicle, potentially saving you from paying extra for the rental company's collision damage waiver.

Here's how credit card rental car insurance works, what it covers and which cards offer some of the best protection.

These cards offer primary rental car coverage on eligible rentals. Coverage can vary by card, rental location and purpose.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

These cards offer primary car rental insurance, as long as you use your card to pay for the entire rental. Note that this isn’t an exhaustive list; you may find other cards offering primary insurance.

The , and each provide primary car rental insurance for rentals of up to 31 consecutive days. The personal cards are primary, while the business card is primary in the U.S. only for business rentals.

This policy covers theft, damage, valid loss-of-use charges, administrative fees and reasonable towing charges due to covered theft or damage.

Policy details vary slightly among the three cards, though. A key difference is the total amount that can be reimbursed for damages caused by theft or collision:

To learn more about each card, read our full reviews for the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve for Business.

The Capital One Venture X and Venture X Business both offer primary rental car insurance, though the coverage terms differ.

The personal Venture X provides reimbursement for theft and collision damage up to the actual cash value of eligible rental vehicles with an original manufacturer's suggested retail price of $75,000 or less. Coverage applies to rentals of up to 15 consecutive days in your country of residence or 31 consecutive days elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the Venture X Business provides primary coverage for eligible rentals made primarily for business purposes, covering theft and collision damage subject to the policy's valuation limits. Rentals of up to 31 consecutive days are eligible for coverage.

To learn more, read our full reviews of the Venture X and Venture X Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

Four of the Ink Business cards from Chase offer primary insurance when you rent for business purposes, providing reimbursement for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less.

Each card provides reimbursement of up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage.

To learn more, read our guide to the Chase Ink Business cards.

United’s cobranded cards offer primary car rental insurance, though the business versions are primary only when you rent for business purposes. You need to decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

This insurance provides reimbursement of up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less.

To learn more, read our guide to the United cards.

Among the most important factors here is making sure you pay for your entire car rental bill with a credit card that has an auto collision damage waiver included in its benefits. You'll also want to decline any insurance offer from your rental car company.

Of course, terms and conditions vary, so always check your card's specific policies before you rent. This way, if you run into a problem, you'll know what's covered and what's not.

If you don’t follow these requirements, your credit card car rental insurance won’t take effect.

Related: All you need to know about using a debit card to rent a car

The car rental insurance from your credit card is technically called an “auto rental collision damage waiver.” This benefit provides reimbursement for damage due to collision or theft. The cash amount your card's insurance policy will cover can vary, so check your card's guide to benefits for specific details.

While some cards also cover loss-of-use and towing charges assessed by the rental company, policies from other credit cards only cover physical damage or theft of the rental vehicle. Knowing what your card will cover is important before you use it.

Additionally, some rental types and locations may not be eligible for coverage. Keep the following provisions in mind if you rely on credit card car rental insurance benefits:

If you have doubts about your car's eligibility, it's best practice to call the customer service number on your card. You can get more information and confirm that your policy covers your rental vehicle type in the country you’ll be visiting.

Related: My experience with Turo: Car rental convenience at a great price

Another important distinction is the difference between primary and secondary car rental insurance, as your card could offer one type or the other. Both types of insurance usually have maximum coverage amounts, so make sure these meet or exceed the total value of the car you’re renting.

If you get into an accident with your rental car and have primary insurance, you only need to file one claim. Generally, primary insurance will reimburse you for the rental car’s cash value or the cost to repair it, whichever is less.

Secondary insurance is different because it only reimburses you for the amount not covered by other types of insurance, such as travel insurance or personal car insurance. However, if you don’t own a car or carry a car insurance policy, most secondary insurance from credit cards will become primary.

Select American Express cards include secondary coverage for damage to or theft of an eligible rental car. If you want primary coverage, you can enroll an eligible Amex card in Premium Car Rental Protection before you rent. Amex charges a flat fee per eligible rental paid for with the enrolled card.

Related: Secondary rental car insurance: Best cards and what's covered

Many consumers focus on the number of points or miles they can earn and redeem when choosing a travel rewards card, but travel protections such as rental car insurance can also provide significant value.

However, reviewing your card’s policy details is essential to understand what is (and isn’t) covered. Don’t assume you’re covered for every possible mishap when you pay for a car rental with a credit card that offers insurance, as many exceptions and exclusions apply.

Ensure you know the details and how they relate to your rental location, vehicle type, length of rental period and other important issues so you won’t be surprised by a bill if your rental car has a problem.

Amadeus has spent decades connecting airlines with travel sellers. AI agents may change how customers shop, but somebody still has to find flights, complete bookings, and handle changes. On its Q3 2026 earnings call on Friday, November 6, an analyst asked why Meta's Muse was using Duffel rather than Amadeus to do that work.

CFO Carol Borg said the Muse-Duffel partnership supports Amadeus' belief that AI platforms will use aggregators rather than build booking systems themselves. She doesn't think it displaces the GDS model: "It actually reinforces it."

But Duffel, not Amadeus, has the direct relationship with Muse. Other companies are pursuing similar roles across airline distribution, hotel booking and payments.

Amadeus used its Q3 2026 earnings call on November 6 to argue that AI platforms will plug into aggregators rather than build their own booking systems, a position CFO Carol Borg said the Meta Muse–Duffel partnership "reinforces." The detail behind that claim is that Duffel, not Amadeus, holds the direct relationship with Muse, even though Duffel's inventory includes direct airline connections, NDC content, and traditional GDS inventory from Travelport. A growing set of intermediaries is taking similar positions: Selfbook powers hotel booking and payments for Perplexity, Nuitée supplies hotel booking infrastructure to Grab and Revolut and is building APIs for AI applications, Katanox has partnered with Selfbook on distribution and settlement, and AirGateway and Kyte offer API-based airline connectivity. CEO Luis Maroto pointed to roughly 3 billion daily searches and said servicing complex itineraries at that scale is harder than connecting to individual airlines. The financials show pricing holding up as volumes slip: bookings fell 2.8% in the first nine months of 2026, which the company attributed largely to Middle East disruption, while revenue per booking rose 5%. Group revenue rose 5.2% at constant currency to €5.08 billion (about $5.67 billion), with adjusted EBIT up 5.5%, and management expects full-year results near the lower end of guidance while maintaining its 2026–2028 targets.

American Express Membership Rewards aren't just for travel anymore. Sports fans now have another way to put their points to use.

As of today, some American Express cardmembers can transfer Membership Rewards points to FanCash, the rewards currency of sports merchandise retailer Fanatics.

The new transfer option is part of a broader partnership between American Express and Fanatics, which also unveiled additional details about its upcoming cobranded credit card.

Eligible U.S. cardmembers can now transfer Membership Rewards points to FanCash at a rate of 1,000 points for $10 in FanCash, giving you a redemption value of 1 cent per point. You can find this option in the newly added Lifestyle section of Amex's transfer partners page.

Simply enter your Fanatics credentials to link your account, which only takes a few seconds.

Once transferred, FanCash can be used toward eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, including sports apparel, trading cards, collectibles and tickets.

However, this isn't necessarily the best use of your Amex points. At 1 cent apiece, you'd be getting just half of TPG's valuation of Membership Rewards points at 2 cents each, a value you can potentially achieve by transferring points to Amex's airline and hotel partners.

Still, this gives sports fans another option for redeeming their points, particularly if they don't have any upcoming travel plans.

Related: Best ways to use Amex Membership Rewards points

As announced earlier this year, American Express and Fanatics are also teaming up on a new cobranded credit card designed for sports fans.

The upcoming Fanatics American Express® Card will have no annual fee and earn 5% FanCash on eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, or 8% or more when shopping through the Fanatics app.

The card will also offer sports-focused perks and more than 500 trading card-inspired designs featuring professional athletes.

It's not yet available for applications, but interested consumers can join the waitlist.

The information for the Fanatics American Express Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The ability to transfer Amex points to FanCash gives sports fans another way to use their rewards, but the 1-cent-per-point value may not appeal to travelers looking to maximize their Membership Rewards points.

For those who regularly shop with Fanatics, however, the new transfer option could be a convenient way to put unused points toward their next purchase.

Meta's Muse AI agent can now book Expedia hotels in the U.S., roughly six weeks after the two companies announced the integration, but the connection is narrower than the announcement suggested. Expedia confirmed to Skift that Muse handles natural-language search and booking while cancellations and changes still route through Expedia customer support, since Expedia is the merchant of record. In a limited Skift test, Muse said it can only book properties with upfront "pay-now" pricing; pay-at-property listings require the agent to use its built-in browser on Expedia's site. Payment runs through Stripe Link, Meta's default option, even when a traveler links an Expedia account — though linking an account unlocks member pricing, which cut one listing's cost by more than $100 versus guest mode. Expedia is adding agentic channels quickly, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Google's AI Mode in the third quarter, and is packaging its technology as a B2B "template" with Qantas as the first partner. The volume isn't there yet: Expedia said it still isn't seeing meaningful traffic from AI, and Booking Holdings CFO Ewout Steenbergen said large language model referrals account for "significantly less than 1%" of Booking.com room nights. CEO Ariane Gorin said the integrations are valuable now mainly as a way to learn how agents make decisions and what tech they require, and that the small volume is high-intent traffic.

Earlier this year, Hard Rock International listed its hotel in New York City on Accor’s booking site and app and told almost no one.

The first month brought 84 room nights. By July, the channel was delivering more than 1,500 a month, more than Hard Rock’s own site produced for the hotel, said Jeff Hook, chief operating officer of Hard Rock. More than 90% of those guests were new to Hard Rock.

Accor and Hard Rock International announced a global partnership on Monday that puts Hard Rock's hotels into Accor's ALL loyalty program, gives Hard Rock access to Accor's global sales team for group and meetings business, and enlists Ennismore, Accor's lifestyle joint venture, to help develop Hard Rock hotels worldwide. No equity changes hands. Accor isn't investing capital, and Chief Commercial, Digital, and Tech Officer Alix Boulnois described the structure as closer to a franchise model in which Accor is paid for the business it brings. The deal follows a quiet test: Hard Rock listed its New York hotel on Accor's site and app earlier this year, and the channel grew from 84 room nights in the first month to more than 1,500 a month by July — more than Hard Rock's own site produced for that hotel, with more than 90% of those guests new to Hard Rock, said Hard Rock COO Jeff Hook. Hook said bookings from Accor's channel are "substantially less expensive" than those from Expedia, Booking.com, or other online travel agencies. Hard Rock will have about 25 standalone hotels in the arrangement, talked to four large hotel companies before choosing Accor, and turned down offers to buy all or part of its hotel division. Ennismore's operational role will vary deal by deal, from finding development deals to full management, with casinos excluded.

Travelers on United Airlines Flight 1252 from Washington to Chicago on Tuesday are in for a surprise.

They will be the first to depart from the spacious new E Gates at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), the first piece of the airport’s more than $20 billion redevelopment and the future center of United’s hub operation at the airport.

“It’s much more spacious,” Andrew Nocella, the chief commercial officer of United, said at a ribbon cutting on Monday. “The gate hold areas are large so there’s plenty of places to sit and there are all kinds of new, great restaurants to enjoy.”

In the news: United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Nocella added: “It’s the tip of the iceberg to the future development of Dulles.”

The redevelopment calls for the extension of the E Gates far to the west with room for up to 50 gates. The rest of IAD will also get a needed upgrade, including the modernization and expansion of Eero Saarinen's iconic terminal, an extension of the AeroTrain and a new international arrivals facility. The aim is to open all of this by the mid-2030s.

“This is the first step to retiring Concourse C-D [and] eliminating mobile lounges — someday," said Jack Potter, the CEO of IAD operator the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

For now, though, the focus at Dulles is on the new E Gates. They're located directly above the AeroTrain station for Concourse C. That is possible because the station was built in 2010, a long walk to the south of the existing Concourse C with the plan to eventually build a concourse above it.

Travelers coming from the train enter the E Gates in a large, high-ceilinged atrium with the new United Club immediately to their right. At 40,000 square feet, the new lounge is the second largest in United's system after the one recently opened at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

United's massive new Houston club: Inside the largest airline lounge in America

The look and feel of the lounge draws its aesthetic from the Washington, D.C., area. The entryway is inspired by the Washington Metro's vaulted subway stations; a cherry blossom mobile hangs in the central seating area; and a Blue Ridge Mountain-themed mural is painted on one of the walls.

"Lounges are very important to our customers," said Nocella. "You can see no design detail was left untouched" in the new E Gates lounge.

From the E Gates atrium, travelers make their way down the concourse itself. Gate areas are interspersed with concessions along the length. And, above, a sterile hallway takes arriving international travelers to the end of the concourse where they can board a mobile lounge to the international arrivals facility in the main terminal.

United will operate both international and domestic flights from the E Gates, Nocella said.

And, for design enthusiasts, the authority used Saarinen's original font for the gate numbers in the new concourse.

The E Gates will allow United to grow its hub at IAD. The airline plans to grow departures by about 20% next summer to around 300 daily flights, up from 250 earlier this year, Nocella said.

United will operate up to roughly 275 departures from IAD in November, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. In June 2027, the number jumps to as many as 290 a day though schedules remain in flux.

What the E Gates will not do is replace the six ground-level gates at the end of Concourse A — gates A1 to A6 — used by United Express regional jets. This was the original plan when the project was approved in the early 2020s.

Instead, United will use the new E Gates to "take the pressure off the C and D facility," Nocella said.

Potter, when asked when the airport authority will close the ground-level A Gates, said: "They’ll stay open until construction has proceeded sufficiently such that they can be relocated."

The authority aims to complete the build out of Concourse E, and the first phase of Concourse G further to the south, by 2030, Potter added.

United plans to expand its IAD hub to around 400 daily departures with all the new gates, Nocella said.

Asked when the airline would grow to 400 departures, he smiled and said they will unveil that at a "different announcement."

Adriana Cisneros sees an opportunity for Venezuela to build a distinctive, conservation-minded tourism industry before the international hotel brands arrive. Whether that vision becomes reality will depend on political stability, security, and crucially, the choices made by the country's tourism leadership.

Venezuela is hardly an obvious candidate for the next great luxury travel destination. #6128. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6127. Dear Robot: How Travel Is (and Isn’t) Talking to AI

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Travel brands invest deeply in AI visibility, but according to Skift's audit of 50 major travel websites' crawler policies, few tell bots where to go — and the directives don't always match who actually gets in. That looks like a shaky starting point, as the rules of AI engagement change.

Travel brands say they want AI to find them. Their websites often tell AI something else, or nothing at all.

That’s the finding of Skift’s review of robots.txt files for 50 major travel sites. These files tell automated programs, or crawlers, whether they’re welcome, and only 10 of the 50 explicitly addressed AI crawlers. The rest lumped them in with every other bot or left them to default settings.

The gap matters more as AI becomes a way travelers shop. In July, Adobe reported that AI visits to travel sites surged 119% year over year. But there’s a “major bottleneck,” according to Adobe analyst Vivek Pandya. “Significant portions of U.S. travel and retail sites remain unreadable to machines, restricting their presence across AI search results,” he wrote in a blog post.

“When an LLM cannot easily read brand content (such as amenities, pricing, or availability),” Pandya added, “potential revenue is being left on the table.”

Skift reviewed robots.txt files — the file that tells automated crawlers whether they're welcome — for 50 major travel sites and found that only 10 explicitly addressed AI crawlers. The other 40 left AI access to catch-all rules or default settings written for other purposes. That gap gained weight on Oct. 30, when Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI backed a proposal that would let a site opt out of AI training by all four with a single robots.txt entry — but only if the site adds it explicitly, since catch-all rules won't carry it. Among the sites that did set AI rules, the pattern favored visibility over training: Expedia and Vrbo give AI search crawlers broad access, Tripadvisor blocks training crawlers while allowing some search access, and Best Western and ITC Hotels explicitly welcome OpenAI's training crawler. Airbnb made the only major change in the sample, moving from allowing GPTBot and ClaudeBot in August to disallowing access across the board by October. Posted policies also diverge from enforcement: eight sites, mainly hotels, returned 403 Forbidden errors to Skift's automated requests, and CraftedStays found Marriott, Hilton, IHG, Hyatt, and Four Seasons name no AI crawler on their banned lists while their bot protection refused fetches outright. Adobe reported in July that AI visits to travel sites surged 119% year over year, and Adobe analyst Vivek Pandya wrote that significant portions of U.S. travel and retail sites remain unreadable to machines, leaving potential revenue on the table.

#6124. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6120. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.
