#6056. The petty joy of a blue election night

Ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”

Shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

So we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

“If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

“You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

Election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

Neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

“What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”

And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

Peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

Most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Big Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood.  On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his new network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

Still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”

Once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

This is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he said.

So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

It was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she said, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”

So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”

That moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he said. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”

But by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

#6054. How America Was Swept by an Anti-Trump Wave

Q&A: How America Was Swept by an Anti-Trump Wave

Was it the Iran war? Corruption? The cost of living? Data centers? By now, everyone has a pet theory to explain why the Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate—and why voters rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. What matters now is how the two sides interpret the results and navigate the political battles to come. And broadly, how the world reacts to the shifting political landscape in the United States.

On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Susan Glasser, a staff writer at the New Yorker and the former editor in chief of Foreign Policy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Was it the Iran war? Corruption? The cost of living? Data centers? By now, everyone has a pet theory to explain why the Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate—and why voters rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. What matters now is how the two sides interpret the results and navigate the political battles to come. And broadly, how the world reacts to the shifting political landscape in the United States.

On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Susan Glasser, a staff writer at the New Yorker and the former editor in chief of Foreign Policy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: I want to start with the big picture. You wrote in your last column: “For now and for forever, the midterm election of 2026 will be known as one of the most decisive rejections of an American president.” Say more.

Susan Glasser: You have to go very far back in history to see a result this explicit, loud, and across-the-board. A lot of people have been comparing it to the post-Watergate elections of 1974 and 1976. If you look at the popular vote, it is the widest midterm margin for Democrats since 1976. Right now, they are trending toward a 13-percentage-point advantage.

However, if you look at the consequences in Congress and how many seats Democrats picked up, you actually have to go much farther back in time to find an election that was this decisive of a swing to either party. The last time this happened was in 1946 and 1948. You have a more than 35-seat pickup for Democrats in the House of Representatives—so far—and as much as an eight-seat pickup in the Senate. That combined House and the Senate pickup hasn’t been seen since the postwar era in American politics.

What’s different about this election compared to other recent ones, such as the 1994 wave that brought Republicans to power in Congress, is that it is a campaign centered around the person of the president, his policies, his leadership, and what he had done with his party. That’s what makes this result so resounding and impactful.

RA: Not in my lifetime have I seen states like Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas come into play in this way for a blue wave.

Many of us were quite stunned to see a post on X from U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance the morning after the election, not only for its speed, but for its analysis. He said, quite simply, “The reason we lost is the [Iran] war.” Do you agree with that?

SG: That was an amazing document. It is pretty much without modern precedent, and I think we have only begun to see what the ramifications of that will be. U.S. President Donald Trump has yet to respond to it, but for a man who has remade the executive branch of the federal government around the single criterion of blind loyalty to him, to have his own vice president attack his signature policy is … wow.

RA: It’s notable that as reporters have looked at how the Iran war has played out in the White House, Vance tends to emerge as the person who was most against the war. He himself is probably the source for many of those claims, so we should take them with a grain of salt, right?

SG: Vance, according to himself, was nobly against this war that is extremely unpopular with the American public. We’re seeing a number of factors at play here. One, Vance is desperately trying to see if there is a path forward for him to run for president in 2028. Two, you will see a number of Republican officeholders and MAGA pundit types like Sean Hannity climbing aboard this argument that it was just the Iran war that lost them the election, because it absolves them of some of the other catastrophes that Trump has wrought on the American public. It’s a convenient foil for them if they can try to win the battle of the narrative around what just happened here.

In my view, the Iran war and the subsequent spike in prices was quite disastrous for Trump and the Republicans politically. However, I believe that this election is a broader repudiation of the Trump administration. That is part of what Vance and Hannity and others are trying to head off.

RA: I agree with you, but just to play devil’s advocate for a minute here: One of the things I think Vance was getting at is that when voters, especially the people who supported Trump in 2024, voted for the Trump campaign’s version of America First, part of that bargain was that there would be no more wars. There’s an argument then that what they really want is just less foreign policy.

The other point to make is that if affordability is the one big-ticket item, which is connected to everything we’re discussing at some level—certainly the Iran war, certainly the tariffs—then how much of what we’ve just seen this week is a secular problem of people swinging from one party to another because they’re unhappy with the current economic conditions? Or how much of it do you think is going to be attributed to the Trump administration’s very unique policies and Trump’s persona?

SG: In politics, as in life, if you start lying to yourself and believing it, you’re in big trouble. Republicans may well come up with an explanation for this election. If it’s a wrong one, or a BS one, they’re going to pay future political consequences.

If you look at a recent Wall Street Journal survey and a number of others, the top issue many Americans said they were bringing to the polls with them wasn’t affordability but corruption. Vance isn’t going to talk about corruption, but we are witnessing the looting of the American presidency on a massive scale. The self-enrichment of our president and a small coterie of his family and other insiders defies all precedent in American history. It’s not partisan to say that people in Kansas are probably pretty offended by the idea of the president of the United States making more than $2 billion off of the presidency in his first year back in office. He himself has admitted it. In an interview earlier this year, he said that he tried to follow the rules—which he didn’t—and it turned out nobody cared.

Corruption has been a powerful force in this election, as it has been in a number of other recent elections this year. The Hungarian election that ousted [Prime Minister] Viktor Orban is one good example, but there are a lot of others. My no. 1 explanation for this election outcome would be the perceived and actual self-enrichment of this out-of-touch leader and his disinterest in the concerns of the electorate around their own economic situation. It encompasses a lot of issues, including taking the country to war. That’s not how our system is supposed to work, for the president to be so disdainful of the country that he doesn’t even feel a need to explain to them why he went to war. There will have to be some fallout from the election.

It wasn’t just Iran. Israel, tariffs, and immigration also loomed large in voters’ minds.

From the Iran war to boat strikes to Ukraine, Democrats now have powerful leverage.

RA: Let’s talk about what next. I’m curious how you think Democrats are going to use this majority in the House and the Senate. What are the topics and items you think they’re going to pursue in their first few months, knowing full well that Trump has already posted on Truth Social an image of a red cap with the word “VETO” on it? There are limits to what they can do, but what are they going to try?

SG: They may be recalibrating because the scale of their victory is so big. I had a conversation a few weeks ago with Chris Coons, who’s going to be the new chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. At that time, he was hopeful that the Democrats would win the majority, but he certainly didn’t think they would have 55 seats. What Democrats may be able to do with 55 seats and a number of centrist Democrats coming in from places like Kansas, North Carolina, and Texas is a different ball game.

The first stop for Democrats looking to affect national security and foreign policy is appropriations bills and the power of the purse. They can attach policy riders on a must-pass defense authorization bill or put provisions into appropriations bills that outline how money can and cannot be spent. Those are things we definitely will see, especially because there’s a real bipartisan consensus, in particular on Ukraine.

I think we will see, at a minimum, much more aggressive efforts to stop Trump from switching sides in the war. I could see some of those very questionable deals that are being discussed between special envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and the Russians—business deals with Russian entities that might enrich Trump insiders and that no American companies actually want—being a quick casualty of this midterm election result.

RA: I’m imagining that the Kremlin is not going to be looking at these results and smiling. I’m sure they’re a bit worried, although simultaneously it’s also clear that Ukraine needs America less today than it did two years ago. They’re trying to become more resilient, and they’re looking at this election quite warily.

I’m curious how you read this election when it comes to shifting attitudes toward Israel, which just had its own elections. What does it mean for broader U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East?

SG: There is a backlash in both parties, interestingly, about Trump’s embrace of [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu and Israel in such an unequivocal way. That’s some of the tone, certainly, of the kind of emergent Vance wing of the party (to the extent there is a Vance wing). There is definitely a backlash in both parties about America’s traditional commitment to Israel in the face of how Netanyahu has prosecuted a scorched-earth war with the Palestinians. That’s true for Democrats in a very dramatic way.

Let’s wait and see what the consequences of Israel’s recent election are. Let’s not forget that they just voted to reject Netanyahu. But given the particularities of that system and his incredible ability to survive, we’ll have to wait and see. Whether Netanyahu or someone else is leading Israel will affect the politics here in Washington.

It’s the Gulf Arabs who have been the engines of a lot of Trump’s foreign policy, not to mention the piggy banks for him and his family. Somebody said to me recently that all the things that we suspect are happening between Putin’s Russia and Trump actually are happening—in terms of vast amounts of sums being directed to Trump and his family—from Gulf interests.

But I think the Gulf Arabs are also very unhappy with Trump. They’re finding out what many others have found out: that Trump doesn’t view relationships as mutual and loyalty is a one-way street with him. Not that long ago, a very senior official from the Middle East asked me: “Why do we have all these American bases and buy all this American military technology to protect ourselves if in fact it’s now the reason that we’re at war? What’s the point of paying the protection money?” It suggests we are at a larger pivot point in the Middle East in terms of geopolitics and the alliances than escaping this narrow quagmire with Iran would suggest. We’re likely looking at a rearrangement of a lot of things in the Middle East in the next two years.

RA: I’m curious how you are thinking about what comes next from the Democratic Party’s side. We’ve all been noting how they won with a very broad tent. There’s a broad slate of candidates, from a Methodist minister in Kansas to a Muslim doctor in Michigan. Are you beginning to detect some coalescing around a coherent foreign policy for the Democrats at this point, or is that a long ways away?

SG: The short answer is “no.” Will Rogers said it a long time ago: “I’m not a member of any organized political party, I’m a Democrat.” Democrats are by definition the more big-tent party in American politics, and they have leaned into that in recent years. Trump spent the last two years campaigning against the very idea of diversity as a strength. So there are some coherent principles that separate these two parties.

Democrats do not have one single coherent view. [Former President Joe] Biden was a backward-looking president in many ways, including with respect to foreign policy. He believed in the possibility of returning to a status quo ante, as a man who was shaped by the foreign-policy debates of the Cold War and perceived threats, opportunities, and alliances through that lens. So there’s a generational shift that’s taking place. I think you’ll see much younger Democratic presidential candidates in 2028. There is also a radical shift in the Senate. This is something people haven’t paid enough attention to. A huge percentage of the Senate is turning over, a much higher percentage than is normal. I think we’re looking at nearly 20 new senators, and the average age of those senators is somewhere in the 50s, and as compared with the average of the people who just left, who would be well into their post-retirement years if they were anybody other than a politician. So a generational shift is definitely going to have consequences on the foreign-policy orientation of the Democrats.

RA: It’s quite literally out with the old.

One thing that we haven’t touched on yet is how this past week could be seen as a repudiation of all the things you’ve said, but also of Big Tech. Elon Musk is the other big loser from this week. He literally poured hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns, and voters have been quite clear: They’ve rejected data centers. They’ve supported candidates who promised regulation.

SG: It is incredible. Five hundred million dollars is more money than has ever been spent on any election by an individual in the history of ours or any country, by a large order of magnitude. That obscene amount of money produced literally zero victories for him. It’s a remarkable moment. It’s one that will be studied. It happened to play right into a campaign theme that Democrats already had across the country, which is a kind of populism of the center slash center-left. It’s this idea that billionaires and a small circle of oligarchic crony capitalists were conspiring with Trump to make sure that they face no legislative or regulatory roadblocks to reinventing the future however they wanted to and in their own self-interest. So this obscene amount of money came at the exact moment when it was already the message for many Democrats around the country.

Does it mean the new Democratic Congress is going to join hands with the Trump administration and regulate artificial intelligence? I’m going to say “no,” in part because the Democratic Congress, as well as the Republican Congress, opted out of any meaningful regulation in the last round of tech innovation in the era of the internet. They basically punted. They talked and talked and never did anything in a meaningful sense. So I’m very pessimistic about major legislation. But I think this could be probably a defining issue, if not the defining issue in the 2028 presidential election. We may be talking a lot less about Trump and a lot more about AI.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#6053. Abdul El-Sayed defeats Mike Rogers despite Haley Stevens drama

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S. Senate seat, a closely watched race that capped off a massive night for progressives.

The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m. Wednesday morning with El-Sayed leading by about seven points.

The candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

The race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

The endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

El-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials said the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

#6050. Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

We finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

The historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

It will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and plans to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

According to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top issue for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a new era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

It’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

As great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that big tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the New Deal agenda.

Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

#6049. Trump names Stephen Miller his chief of staff ahead of Dem takeover

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president’s last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration’s domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”

Wiles, who Trump recently announced had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I’ll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don’t like what they’re doing… They’ve already called and they want to talk about things. And that’s fine.”

Trump summoned Thursday’s press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with “VETO” across the front in large white lettering.

Miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump’s first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. “Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once said the party is “unworthy of power.”

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller said during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”

#6047. MAGA media scrambles to form a circular firing squad

Forty-five minutes before the first polls closed on Tuesday, Greg Gutfeld was still doing what Fox News does best, acknowledging reality just long enough to replace it with a culture-war hallucination. “Gas prices are so high, I’m going to vote for the party that wanted to trans my kids,” he joked on “The Five,” adding that he didn’t see Democratic wins on the horizon. “There is no blue wave materializing,” Clay Travis, the Outkick founder and Fox contributor, posted at 3 p.m. EST, adding that Republicans were surging in Florida and the polls were about to be proven wrong yet again.

Then the polls closed, and MAGA’s delusions were pulverized. The country that right-wing media had spent two years describing as angry, ascendant and permanently realigned voted in an avalanche that crushed years of manufactured MAGA hype. American voters told the president to take his $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks and shove them. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to get away from Democrats and then spent a reported $150 million to deliver the Lone Star State for Republicans, saw his early Tuesday post urging people to vote red disappear from his profile by Wednesday.

The country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman governor in American history. Michigan sent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Washington as the first Muslim senator. New Hampshire elected Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man in the Senate. New Mexico made Deb Haaland the first Native American woman governor, and Peggy Flanagan became Minnesota’s first Native American woman senator. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott — the state’s first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Ohio got its first woman governor in Dr. Amy Acton. South Carolina tapped Dr. Annie Andrews as its first elected woman senator. Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in 94 years. While votes are still being counted in key races, solid majorities in both the Senate and House are assured, and Democrats are set to make Hakeem Jeffries the country’s first Black speaker.

Even the New York Post, Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid and a loyal Trump house organ, refused to mince words on its front page: “Trump suffers historic rebuke as Dems romp in midterms,” with “BLUE TSUNAMI” blaring beneath it. On “Fox and Friends” Wednesday morning, Ainsley Earhart warned viewers that “your wallet and your way of life” are now in the crosshairs.

The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment.

It is no surprise that Trump 2.0, stripped of its previous establishment Republican guardrails like Mike Pence and Mitch McConnell, has culminated in such total structural collapse. The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment. Right-wing media spent years confusing its ability to dominate a conversation with its ability to represent a country. When Tuesday’s returns exposed the difference, its leading voices reached for almost everything except accountability. They blamed immigration. They blamed insufficient restrictions on voting. They blamed each other. Alex Jones even decided Trump might secretly be a Democrat.

For the network’s election night coverage, Fox News seated former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio between two of Trump’s former press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt, and he told them to their faces that they were “missing the plot.” He said, “The American people are looking at a war they do not believe in, and they did not authorize. They’re looking at prices that are making it impossible for middle-class people, let alone working-class people, to live.”

Trump, watching at the White House, raged on Truth Social — “Why does FoxNews have deBlasio” — and seethed at the panel’s lone liberal: “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me.” After Gutfeld read the president’s text on air — which is as good a diagram as exists of what Fox News is now: a suggestion box the president monitors live — Tarlov answered on X, not on Truth Social: “Reality is a tricky thing,” and the president “should get better at dealing with it.”

On Newsmax, things were somehow worse. Political strategist Dick Morris argued that Trump’s problem was effectively excessive success: He had solved the major problems that would otherwise motivate Republican voters. The influencer ecosystem, meanwhile, went straight for the circular firing squad, and every faction picked a different target.

Jones, livestreaming as the returns buried his movement, said Trump himself is the plant: “I think he’s a Democrat. I’m 100% at war with Trump. He’s not that r*tarded. He did this on purpose. I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them.” Benny Johnson and Libs of TikTok reached for the great replacement theory, and Fox’s Lawrence Jones supplied the broadcast version, surveying Texas and concluding, “Texas, there is a lesson here. Don’t be so welcoming.”

So much for celebrating people voting with their feet and the U-Hauls leaving California.

Laura Loomer went straight doomer: “America is over and so is the American Dream.” Others blamed Sen. John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE Act and shrink the electorate further, as though the answer to such a broad repudiation were fewer voters. The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro posted the “everything is fine” fire GIF — “Just checking in to see how things are goi—” — and the Federalist’s Sean Davis answered with the hot-dog-suit meme, the one where the man in the costume insists everyone else is the problem.

The recriminations got personal fast. Rep. Nancy Mace told Fox’s Mark Levin to “STFU,” blamed his “beloved” war for the losses and called the night “devastating . . . for the hard-working American who can’t afford to buy a home, or fill their tank with gas or put food on the table.” Levin returned fire: Mace was a “washed up political loser” and “one of the most mentally unhinged POS to ever be in Congress.” She was angry, he said, “because you’ll actually have to now work for a living . . . Good riddance, crackpot.” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis gloated that with governors’ races lost in Texas and Ohio and Georgia, the Sunshine State would stand alone among the ten most populous states with a Republican governor. And Katie Miller — podcaster, administration wife, professional MAGA explainer — told CBS’s Norah O’Donnell that she had not voted at all. “I did not vote in Virginia because in Virginia when you vote, you dox your own address, and so I prefer my own safety and security over giving that up.”

In the end, the movement’s loudest voices spent the cycle performing for each other. Some of them couldn’t even be bothered to vote.

#6046. Do the Democrats Have a Cohesive Economic Plan?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Q&A: Do the Democrats Have a Cohesive Economic Plan?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

This week’s congressional elections in the United States saw a historic shift toward Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, including wins in traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. But with President Donald Trump still in the White House and Democrats still trying to give shape to their own agenda, the implications for economic policy remain unclear.

Was the election outcome primarily fueled by inflation? What are the implications for the AI industry? And what macroeconomic options do the Democrats now have?

This week’s congressional elections in the United States saw a historic shift toward Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, including wins in traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. But with President Donald Trump still in the White House and Democrats still trying to give shape to their own agenda, the implications for economic policy remain unclear.

Was the election outcome primarily fueled by inflation? What are the implications for the AI industry? And what macroeconomic options do the Democrats now have?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: What is the relationship between a political event of this magnitude and mundane cost-of-living issues, which most Americans seem to have been bothered by? Is this the stuff that political tsunamis are made of?

Adam Tooze: The cost-of-living issue, and the continuous shocks of price increases and the felt experience of the exorbitant level of prices, has probably not been as pressing as it is in the current moment in many parts of the U.S. since the 1970s. So at that level, there’s a kind of epochal quality to this. And the other thing surely to say is that nor have we had a government, an administration and a supportive Congress, so blithely refusing to simply take seriously any of those issues in a meaningful way. And it’s that combination, I think, which creates this outcome. It would have been damaging to everyone’s sort of self-understanding as a rational political analyst if something like this outcome had not happened.

Because how can you have this level of dissatisfaction over prices and price increases and a government committed to protectionism, to starting a war, to incredibly unequal tax breaks, to promoting a growth model that is so K-shaped, that is so promoting a wealth inequality, and not get a backlash? That would have tested the ongoing debate about whether the ’90s formula, “It’s the economy, stupid”—this would really have put a stake through the heart of that theory with garlic on top if we had not seen this backlash.

CA: This kind of epochal shift inevitably sparks debates about new, or renewed, political taxonomies in the United States. The term that is now being used to describe many of the new senators and governors elected by Democrats in unlikely places is “prairie populism.” And I’m curious what that term might mean when it comes to economic policy?

AT: Going all the way back to the late 19th century, there has been a brand of radical, challenging, anti-status quo politics, in contrast to socialism, which was populism. Populism came out of the prairie, out of the Midwest of the prairie states of the agricultural constituency, because it was about the way in which the gilded age economy in the United States was rigged in the interests of coastal elites—basically New York and the East coast elite.

And that’s the echo that’s being picked up on in this sort of talk. It’s a little exaggerated because there’s a huge difference between present day consumer orientated cost of living type of politics and the sort of radicalism, the deep structural changes that late 19th-century populists were demanding—who were really challenging the fundamental structures of the American political economy of that moment. And I do think that’s one of the fundamental questions for the Democrats right now, is that coming out of the midterms of 2018—which were also a Democratic breakthrough, against the first Trump presidency, though not on the current scale—there was a real sense that the discourse of American politics shifted. You got figures like Jake Sullivan spiraling to the top of the democratic pile on an agenda that was an explicit break in neoliberalism.

And I don’t quite know where that goes right now, whether there is a mood on the large part of the Democratic Party to resume that kind of quite more fundamental questioning of the orthodoxies or whether we take all that for granted now and we’re going to just focus on trying to deliver. I think we haven’t quite got the bearings yet of what this victory means. It was predicted, but I haven’t so far seen on the part of the Democrats a kind of coherent, new, comprehensive agenda—even in the sense of defining what its limits would be and how far one wants to go—emerging at this point.

CA: Polls suggest that many voters in the United States share skepticism about artificial intelligence and the role it’s playing in the economy, specifically the proliferation of data centers. What is the future of AI potentially with this new Democratic-controlled Congress?

AT: It’s been quite something to behold, the anxiety running through Wall Street over the last couple of days and kind of climaxing last night about the potential threat to the data center build out. Because America’s path to the AI future is very compute heavy. It’s all about data center build outs. And if you look at the states where this is happening, apart from Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, I think the central play is Texas. And there was a real lot of big tech money mobilized on this issue of trying to ensure that a group of AI friendly politicians were elected.

And on the contrary then, the groundswell of Democratic mobilization was around AI and data centers as kind of a bundling issue, right? It’s about local pollution from the noise and everything else. It’s about local electricity rates and the impact that these huge consumers have on local energy prices. And it’s about AI as AI, its direct role on the labor market. And it’s about AI as the symbol of an irresponsible, unanswerable kind of oligarchy that just stamps itself on the face of American society. And these were a very powerful combination.

And I think Wall Street analysts were counting 40 or 41 local referenda, local motions that are being passed. All of which I think went to the anti-AI side. And in Texas, we’re talking about 60 gigawatts of buildouts, so an absolutely gigantic buildout valued at $200 billion, I think. And now the Democrats have a much more powerful hold on Texas politics than any time recently. And as we know, in the regional political economy of the United States, Texas and Florida are two great red state counter-examples to the New York and California visions of America’s future. And so for this break to happen is really very dramatic.

And it does form a connection between this electoral result and the market. On the morning after the election, though the S&P 500 as a whole was doing fine, Tesla had sold off, CoreWeave, all of these cloud companies have sold off quite hard. Trump’s media platforms are down, unsurprisingly. So it does look as though there is a selective shakeout happening across stock that are very exposed on the AI issue, very exposed to this blowback and are, in any case, over the last couple of months, looking increasingly fragile from a financial point of view.

CA: Democrats are promising to make life for ordinary Americans more affordable, but how they’ll do that is still somewhat of an open question. On a macroeconomic level, could finding a way to lower interest rates be something that Democrats in Congress turn their attention to?

AT: I think this is a really interesting question. I mean, there’s a real tension between projects of trying to address the cost of living crisis through concrete interventions on particular prices and market structure and price gouging on drugs and microeconomic policy strategies and the bigger macroeconomic picture.

And of course, Congress doesn’t shape that bigger macroeconomic picture. Really except through fiscal policy. It doesn’t have a direct influence on interest rates. If it wants to see interest rates come down, the way to do that, presumably, would be to adopt tough fiscal policy. It doesn’t necessarily mean you slash spending, but you would need to raise taxes and you’d need to actually build a coalition that was willing to do that. And there’s lots of ways of doing that in a progressive way. But that’s not something the Democrats have been keen to do recently, really, is to push redistributional taxes. Or you have to put the Fed in a position where it has no option but to do various very unconventional interventions. Which again is perfectly logical and sensible from a left Keynesian point of view. But it’s a breach of the kind of orthodoxy which the Democrats have embraced all the time outside moments of absolute crisis.

So I do think this question of what the agenda of the Democrats is really, macroeconomically, is quite unclear. Because we’re clearly no longer in the Larry Summers Bill Clinton 1990s era. We left that behind in the Biden administration. What the agenda, what the paradigm now is I think is very open-ended. Take the issue of AI. One of the effects of the AI boom is to suck foreign money into the American equity markets. It’s one of the fundamental ways in which the American balance payments now currently balances. If that goes away—and there’s very good reasons for wanting to embrace that as American’s future, slow this down, try and close the two legs of the K-shaped economy—the most likely prediction is that the dollar depreciates, the dollar devalues.

And again, you’ll find people saying, Well, that will be great for industrial policy, that’s exactly what we need, American producers are more competitive, who needs tariffs if you have a devaluing dollar? But the dollar is also American purchasing power. And so if the dollar devalues appreciably, seriously, this raises the price of American imports. It raises the cost of buying foreign goods for American consumers. It isn’t a way to increase purchasing power and address the cost-of-living crisis. It does the opposite, right? It restricts imports by way of raising the price of foreign goods.

Now, this isn’t one-to-one or simple, but there’s just a series of tensions here that are not squarely addressed at the current moment. There hasn’t been any cause to address them, though I also think there was an agenda around the Biden administration that pretty clearly spelled out some of the trade-offs here. For instance, we would intentionally slow down the renewable energy surge in the U.S. because it involved Chinese solar panels and that wasn’t the top priority, actually.

So what are the new priorities? What is the new set? If the cost of living is the absolute priority over everything else, then you would think that a radical free trade agenda would be the way to go. But Congress can’t do that without a compliant White House. And which Democrat is actually going to run on that, given what we know the Biden administration did, which was to maintain Trump’s tariffs from the first administration? And big parts of the Democratic coalition, notably what’s left of the blue collar trade unions, are, shall we say, pro-tariff, broadly speaking. Not Trump’s crazy ones, but they are not interested in ensuring that American consumers can have the cheapest possible affordable family car. That’s not their agenda. So there’s a whole series of really quite complicated trade-offs here that will have to be faced again.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi

Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze

#6042. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

Florida narrowly missed the quake, with Republicans winning all the major statewide races by the thinnest of margins. The one-time quintessential purple state, a so-goes-the-nation bellwether with a relatively even amount of registered Republicans and Democrats, turned remarkably red in the Trump era following Barack Obamaâs back-to-back wins in 2008 and 2012. The state legislature redrew its maps to enshrine a supermajority, and a post-Covid influx of GOP transplants seeking lower taxes and lax regulations shifted the balance significantly. A Democrat hasnât made a fight of the governorâs race this decade, and no Democratic Senate candidate has come close to winning since Bill Nelson lost his reelection bid in 2018.

Angie Nixon felt different. The Jacksonville organizer and bookstore owner ran a proudly democratic socialist campaign, advocating for universal healthcare in a state beset by multiple insurance crises and affordability issues. #6037. Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

Waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”

Reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”)

Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

Not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

But this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

What Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

But it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

What’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion shows maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

If America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.
